config.title: Micro-frontend Shell

intro.title: Micro-frontend Shell
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a micro-frontend shell application, which acts as a main container that loads and displays multiple smaller, independent frontend applications (micro-frontends). You will learn how to use React with TypeScript to create a shell component that dynamically renders these micro-frontends based on user navigation. The core programming concepts involve component composition, state management for routing, and type-safe props using TypeScript interfaces. You'll work with React hooks like useState to manage the active micro-frontend and conditional rendering to switch between them. By the end, you'll have a foundational shell that can integrate separate frontend modules, a key pattern in modern scalable web development.
intro.usecase: Micro-frontend shells are used in large-scale applications like e-commerce platforms where different teams own separate sections—product listings, shopping cart, user reviews—that must integrate seamlessly. Enterprise dashboards at companies like Salesforce or Microsoft use this pattern to combine analytics, CRM tools, and reporting modules into a unified interface. This approach allows independent deployment of features like payment processing or inventory management while maintaining a cohesive user experience.

objectives: Construct a React shell component to serve as the main container for micro-frontends.
Initialize and manage application state to control which micro-frontend is displayed.
Implement a navigation handler to switch between different micro-frontend modules.
Configure dynamic import paths to load micro-frontends on demand.
Render micro-frontend components conditionally based on the current application state.
Integrate routing logic to map navigation events to specific micro-frontend views.
Apply TypeScript interfaces to define the structure and props for micro-frontend modules.

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and useState from 'react' to enable component creation and state management.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The imports are added at the top of the file, making React and useState available for use.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. Remember to import both React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Define the MicroFrontendShell component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named MicroFrontendShell that returns JSX. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.hint: Start by defining the component after your imports. Remember to return JSX (like a div or fragment) from the component body.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the MicroFrontendShell component here
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a MicroFrontendShell component defined that returns JSX.
successCriteria: The MicroFrontendShell component is defined and returns valid JSX.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started defining the component, but make sure it returns JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Check that you've named it MicroFrontendShell and it returns JSX.

steps.title: Define the micro-frontend configuration type
steps.instruction: Inside the component file, create a TypeScript interface named MicroFrontendConfig with two properties: name (string) and url (string).
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions with type annotations.
steps.expectedOutcome: The interface will define the shape for micro-frontend configuration objects used later in the lesson.
successCriteria: A MicroFrontendConfig interface exists with name: string and url: string properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your interface has both 'name' and 'url' properties with string types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Remember to use the 'interface' keyword with the correct property names and types.

steps.title: Initialize the active micro-frontend state
steps.instruction: Inside the MicroFrontendShell component, use the useState hook to declare a state variable named activeMicroFrontend with an initial value of null. The state should be typed to hold either a string (for the micro-frontend name) or null.
steps.hint: Use useState with a generic type like useState<string | null>(null).
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: state for a selected item
const [selectedItem, setSelectedItem] = useState<string | null>(null);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a state variable to track which micro-frontend is currently active.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with an initial value of null and typed as string | null, and the state variable is named activeMicroFrontend.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure to use useState with the correct generic type (string | null) and name the variable activeMicroFrontend.
steps.feedbackWrong: declare a state variable inside the component using useState.

steps.title: Add the shell container structure
steps.instruction: Return a JSX structure from your component that includes a container div with a header, main content area, and navigation sections.
steps.hint: Start by returning a div element that wraps the entire layout. Inside, add a header, a main section, and a nav element for navigation.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a JSX structure with a container div containing header, main, and nav elements, forming the basic layout for the micro-frontend shell.
successCriteria: The component returns a div element containing a header, a main, and a nav element in JSX.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your component returns a div containing header, main, and nav elements in JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component should return JSX with a container div that includes header, main, and nav elements. Check your return statement.

steps.title: Display the active micro-frontend name
steps.instruction: Inside the component's return statement, add a header element that displays the name of the currently active micro-frontend from the state.
steps.hint: Use the activeMicroFrontend state variable inside JSX curly braces to display its value. You can use an <h2> or similar heading element.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will now show a header displaying the active micro-frontend name when state is set.
successCriteria: A header element (like <h2>) is added inside the return statement that displays the activeMicroFrontend state value using JSX curly braces.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a header, but make sure it displays the activeMicroFrontend state value using curly braces like {activeMicroFrontend}.
steps.feedbackWrong: The header isn't displaying the active micro-frontend name. Check that you're using the activeMicroFrontend state variable inside JSX curly braces.

steps.title: Create navigation buttons for each micro-frontend
steps.instruction: Inside the component's return statement, map over the microFrontendConfigs array to create a button for each micro-frontend configuration.
steps.hint: Use the .map() method on microFrontendConfigs. Each button should display the micro-frontend name and call selectMicroFrontend with that name when clicked.
steps.expectedOutcome: The shell container will display three navigation buttons labeled 'Dashboard', 'Settings', and 'Profile' that can be clicked to select different micro-frontends.
successCriteria: The .map() method is used on microFrontendConfigs to generate buttons, each button has a unique key, displays the micro-frontend name, and calls selectMicroFrontend with that name when clicked.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that each button has a unique key prop, displays the micro-frontend name, and calls selectMicroFrontend with the correct name when clicked.
steps.feedbackWrong: The navigation buttons aren't properly created. Make sure to use .map() on microFrontendConfigs to generate buttons, and ensure each button has the required key, content, and onClick handler.

steps.title: Wire button clicks to the select handler
steps.instruction: Add onClick handlers to each button in the navigation section that call selectMicroFrontend with the appropriate micro-frontend name.
steps.hint: Use the onClick prop on each button element and pass the config.name to selectMicroFrontend.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: wiring a button click
<button onClick={() => handleSelect(item.id)}>Select Item</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: Each navigation button will now trigger the selectMicroFrontend handler with its corresponding micro-frontend name when clicked.
successCriteria: All three navigation buttons have onClick handlers that call selectMicroFrontend with the appropriate config.name.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some onClick handlers, but not all buttons are properly wired. Make sure each button calls selectMicroFrontend with its config.name.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons don't have proper onClick handlers yet. Each button needs an onClick that calls selectMicroFrontend with the corresponding micro-frontend name.
